contributions.headingText: Adenosarcoma is a biphasic neoplasm composed of a benign epithelial component and a malignant stromal component.
2B5D.1 & XH5544 Malignant mixed epithelial and mesenchymal tumour of corpus uteri & Adenosarcoma

In addition to occurring in the uterus, these tumours also occur in the cervix and the vagina (see section Adenosarcoma of the uterine cervix and section Adenosarcoma of the vagina). Additionally, these tumours may be extrauterine, presumably arising from endometriosis (see section Adenosarcoma of the ovary).
Patients present with abnormal uterine bleeding, an enlarged uterus, a pelvic mass, or tissue protruding through the cervical os. A history indicating recurrent polyps is not uncommon.
There is a wide age range, but patients are most often postmenopausal.
This neoplasm is presumed to arise from neoplastic transformation of a Müllerian mesenchymal cell {26592504} that subsequently stimulates reactive growth of benign companion glands.
The pathogenesis is unknown, but some cases are associated with tamoxifen use {8811383}.

The tumours are typically solitary, exophytic, polypoid masses filling the endometrial cavity (mean size: ~5–6 cm) {2156771; 18941402}; they commonly prolapse through the cervical os. They may resemble typical endometrial polyps when small. With large adenosarcomas, necrosis and haemorrhage are common, particularly in the setting of sarcomatous overgrowth.

Classically, the tumour has phyllodiform cleft-like or dilated glands (rigid cysts) lined by benign endometrial or ciliated epithelium surrounded by a distinct cuff of neoplastic stroma, which is typically hypercellular relative to nearby benign tissue {2156771}. Stromal proliferation and atypia are generally present but may be quite subtle. The sarcomatous component is most often nondescript homologous type, but rhabdomyosarcomatous differentiation is possible and sex cord differentiation is rare. The sarcomatous component may overgrow the epithelial component (referred to as sarcomatous overgrowth); there may also be transformation to high-grade sarcoma. The epithelial component may display some cytological atypia and frequently has metaplastic changes. Immunohistochemically, the tumours are often positive for CD10, ER, and PR, although these are often negative in sarcomatous overgrowth {18469708; 18941402}. The diagnosis of adenofibroma has been removed from this edition of the WHO classification, and it is believed that the majority of tumours previously diagnosed as adenofibromas are simply low-grade adenosarcomas {25118811; 26715175; 20179434} or benign endometrial or cervical polyps with unusual morphology (i.e. focal phyllodes-like architecture and/or increased stromal cellularity surrounding glands).

This neoplasm lacks the genomic aberrations and specific chromosomal rearrangements found in other gynaecological sarcomas {25231023}. Amplification of 8q13 and high-level copy-number gains of MYBL1 are seen in some cases, most often associated with sarcomatous overgrowth {26974998; 25231023}. A small subset of cases harbour NCOA2/3 fusions {26592504}. TP53 mutation, which is uncommon, is associated with sarcomatous overgrowth and aggressive behaviour {25231023; 11240741; 28834809}.

Essential: proliferation of malignant stroma accompanied by non-neoplastic Müllerian epithelium usually forming broad, leaf-life structures projecting into cystic spaces, resembling phyllodes tumour of breast; periglandular cuffing of hypercellular stroma; stromal mitotic activity (can be minimal or absent).
The staging of adenosarcoma differs from that of other uterine sarcomas; designation as pT1 is based on the presence and depth of myometrial invasion, not tumour size.

The prognosis is generally favourable compared with that of other gynaecological sarcomas. Sarcomatous overgrowth, deep myometrial invasion, and extrauterine recurrence are adverse prognostic variables. High-grade atypia may also portend a worse outcome {28834809}.
